title: Why does your brain trick you?
outcome: The student will be able to explain how our brains use shortcuts to make quick decisions and why these can lead to mistakes.
subject: general

concepts.title: Why does your brain trick you?
concepts.centralCause: The brain uses mental shortcuts (heuristics) to process information quickly, which can lead to biased judgments when the situation is complex.
conditions: The brain is trying to save energy or time

cards.title: The Brain's Shortcut System

fact.statement: Your brain uses shortcuts to make decisions quickly because thinking deeply takes too much energy.
conditions: When you have to make a fast choice
fact.source: Generated from model knowledge, not checked

hook.question: Why does your brain choose the easy path instead of the perfect one?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if you have unlimited time to think. Tell me why.

cards.explanation: Think of your brain like a busy office. To keep things moving, it uses 'shortcuts' called heuristics. These are mental rules of thumb. For example, if you see a dark cloud, you assume it will rain. You don't wait to see a raindrop first. This saves your brain from getting tired by over-analyzing every tiny detail.

action.instruction: Imagine you are looking at a fruit basket. You have to pick a fruit in 1 second. Now, imagine you have 1 minute to look at every fruit. Predict which way you will choose more often and why.
constants: The goal of picking a fruit

question.prompt: If you see a person wearing a lab coat in a park, why might you assume they are a doctor?

key.expectedCause: The brain uses a shortcut by linking the lab coat to a doctor because it's a fast way to categorize people.
acceptable: It's a mental shortcut to save time

key.typicalMistake: They are a doctor because they have a white coat.
key.followUp: Does this shortcut always work, or can it be wrong?

cards.title: The Power of First Impressions

fact.statement: People tend to rely too much on the first piece of information they see (Anchoring).
conditions: When a number or idea is presented first
fact.source: Generated from model knowledge, not checked

hook.question: Why does the first number you hear stay stuck in your head?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if you hear a second, much higher number. Tell me why.

cards.explanation: This is called 'Anchoring.' Your brain grabs onto the first piece of information it sees and uses it as a starting point. Even if that first piece of information isn't very important, your brain uses it as a 'hook' to judge everything else that follows.

action.instruction: Imagine a shop sells a toy for $100. Then they show you a toy for $50. Now, imagine the shop shows you a toy for $10 first, then the $50 one. Predict which toy feels like a better deal.
constants: The final price of the second toy

question.prompt: If a store shows you a $1,000 watch first, then a $200 watch, why does the $200 watch seem like a bargain?

acceptable: The first number sets a starting point in your mind
Your brain compares the second price to the first one
key.typicalMistake: Because $200 is a smaller number than $1,000.
key.followUp: Can you think of a time a salesperson might use this on you?

cards.title: The Groupthink Trap

fact.statement: People often agree with a group even when they have doubts (Conformity).
conditions: When the person feels pressure to fit in
fact.source: Generated from model knowledge, not checked

hook.question: Why do we sometimes say 'yes' when we actually mean 'no'?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if you are alone in a room. Tell me why.

cards.explanation: Conformity happens because our brains want to belong. It feels safe to agree with the group because being 'different' can feel lonely or scary. Your brain chooses the easy path of fitting in rather than the harder path of standing out, especially when the group is large.

action.instruction: Imagine you are in a group of 10 people. Everyone says the sky is green. Now, imagine you are the only person in the room. Predict which situation makes you more likely to agree that the sky is green.
action.changedCondition: The number of people in the group
constants: The fact that the sky is not green

cards.title: The Confirmation Bias

fact.statement: We tend to notice information that agrees with what we already believe.
conditions: When we already have a strong opinion
fact.source: Generated from model knowledge, not checked

hook.question: Why is it so easy to ignore facts that prove us wrong?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if you only look for information that supports your favorite team. Tell me why.

cards.explanation: This is called Confirmation Bias. Your brain likes being right! It feels good to have a steady belief. To save energy, your brain ignores 'confusing' information that disagrees with your beliefs and highlights information that makes you feel like you were right all along.

action.instruction: Imagine you believe all dogs are mean. You see a dog wagging its tail. Now, imagine you believe all dogs are friendly. You see the same dog wagging its tail. Predict how your brain treats the same dog in both cases.
constants: The observation of the tail wagging

question.prompt: If you believe a certain fruit is delicious, why might you only remember the times you enjoyed it and forget the times it tasted bad?

key.expectedCause: Because of confirmation bias, your brain focuses on the info that fits your belief and ignores the rest.
acceptable: Your brain is looking for proof that you are right
It's easier to remember things that agree with your opinion
key.typicalMistake: Because I just forgot the bad times.
key.followUp: How can I make sure I'm seeing the whole truth?

criteria.example: Confirmation bias makes me focus on the good times because they fit my belief.

cards.title: Mastering Your Mind

fact.statement: Recognizing these biases helps you make smarter, more independent choices.
conditions: When you pause to think before deciding
fact.source: Generated from model knowledge, not checked

hook.question: How can you become the boss of your own brain?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if you stop and think for 10 seconds before making a big choice. Tell me why.

cards.explanation: To beat these biases, you need to 'pause.' When you feel a sudden urge to agree with a group, or when you see a number that feels like a trap, stop. Ask yourself: 'Is my brain taking a shortcut here?' By slowing down, you give your conscious mind a chance to look at the facts instead of just following a mental shortcut.

action.instruction: Imagine you see a 'Limited Time Offer' sign for a toy you don't really need. Imagine you see a 'Sale' sign for a toy you do need. Predict which one requires you to pause and think more to avoid a bias.
constants: The act of looking at the sign
